cards.back: A class that owns a page's locators and actions, so a UI change needs one fix and tests read as user behaviour.

cards.front: Why can a page object create locators in its constructor before the page has loaded?
cards.back: Creating a locator doesn't touch the browser. It's resolved each time it's used.

cards.front: Why should a page object expose a locator instead of returning `textContent()`?
cards.back: `textContent()` reads once. A locator lets the test use a web-first assertion such as `toHaveText()`, which retries.

cards.front: Does Playwright enforce `private` and `readonly` when it runs tests?
cards.back: No. It removes types without checking them, so run `tsc --noEmit` in CI.

cards.front: What does `{ box: true }` do on `test.step()`?
cards.back: It reports a failure at the line in the test that called the step, not at a line inside the helper.

cards.front: Which `trace` value keeps traces only for failed tests?
cards.back: `retain-on-failure`. The value `on-failure` is silently accepted and records nothing.

cards.front: Why re-export `expect` from your fixtures file?
cards.back: A spec then needs one import. Importing `expect` from two modules is a syntax error.

cards.front: Why use a builder function instead of a shared data object?
cards.back: Each call returns a new object, so a change made by one test can't leak into the next test in that worker.

cards.front: Why put test data cleanup in a fixture?
cards.back: Code after `use()` runs even when the test fails.

cards.front: How do you make a date-dependent test stable?
Two `page.route()` handlers match the same URL. Which one answers?
How can a mock stay close to the real API?
cards.back: Call `route.fetch()` for the real response, change only what the test needs, and pass it to `route.fulfill()`.
